name: Types of Attention
what: This subtopic covers the definition of attention and the three main types: sustained, divided, and selective. It also distinguishes between internal and external stimuli as the two sources of information that attention can be directed toward.
why: Understanding the different types of attention helps explain why we can concentrate on some tasks but not others, and why multitasking often reduces performance. These concepts underpin much of how humans navigate complex environments.

items.title: I can define attention and explain its general purpose
items.what: Attention is the process of actively focusing on particular information while simultaneously ignoring other information. It allows us to direct limited mental resources toward the most relevant stimuli.
items.why: Without attention, we would be overwhelmed by every stimulus in our environment and unable to complete tasks or respond meaningfully to the world.
items.example: A student in a noisy cafeteria focuses on reading their notes before an exam, tuning out surrounding conversations.

items.title: I can distinguish between internal and external stimuli
items.what: Internal stimuli originate from within the body, such as hunger, pain, or a thought. External stimuli originate from outside the body, such as a conversation, a sound, or something seen.
items.why: Both types of stimuli compete for our attention at all times, so identifying their source helps explain why attention can be disrupted by things as varied as a headache or a loud noise.
items.example: While writing an essay, a student is distracted by both a headache (internal stimulus) and music playing nearby (external stimulus).

items.title: I can define sustained attention and describe its three stages
items.what: Sustained attention is the ability to focus on one stimulus or task across a prolonged, continuous period of time. It involves three stages: focusing attention on the stimulus, maintaining that attention, and then releasing it when no longer needed.
items.why: Many daily tasks require sustained attention to be completed accurately, and understanding its stages helps explain when and why attention breaks down.
items.example: A student completing a 45-minute exam paper must focus on each question, maintain attention across the full period, and release it when they hand in their paper.

items.title: I can explain the effect of distraction on sustained attention
items.what: Distractions are internal or external stimuli that draw attention away from the current task. They force an individual to repeatedly refocus, which reduces the effectiveness of sustained attention, particularly when the task is boring or when the person is fatigued.
items.why: Recognising how distraction impairs sustained attention explains why study environments and task engagement matter for cognitive performance.
items.example: A student trying to memorise notes while their phone keeps buzzing must refocus repeatedly, making the study session less efficient than one without interruptions.

items.title: I can define divided attention and identify when it is used
items.what: Divided attention involves splitting attention across two or more stimuli or tasks at the same time, which is the basis of multitasking. It tends to be more successful when at least one of the tasks is automatic or easy.
items.why: Divided attention is common in everyday life, but understanding its limits helps explain why performance on complex tasks decreases when we try to do multiple things at once.
items.example: A student takes notes from the board while simultaneously listening to the teacher explain a concept, dividing attention between two related tasks.

items.title: I can explain the negative implications of multitasking on performance
items.what: Multitasking can reduce performance when tasks are complex, unrelated, or use different platforms or mediums. Switching between tasks increases distractibility and reduces depth of understanding.
items.why: People often overestimate their multitasking ability; understanding its costs supports better decisions about how to allocate attention during study or work.
items.example: Writing an essay while online shopping results in slower writing, less coherent arguments, and missed ideas because both tasks compete for limited attentional resources.

items.title: I can define selective attention and provide examples of it in action
items.what: Selective attention involves exclusively focusing on one specific stimulus or task while ignoring all others, acting as a filter on both external stimuli (other sounds, sights) and internal stimuli (thoughts, emotions).
items.why: Selective attention is essential for prioritising what is most relevant in complex or busy environments where many stimuli are present simultaneously.
items.example: At a crowded party, a person focuses entirely on the conversation they are having, filtering out the many other voices and music in the room.
